newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court to hear case of pregnant glue-sniffer.
newsitem.headline: Canada court to hear case of pregnant glue-sniffer.

text.p: The Canadian Supreme Court agreed on Friday to consider whether the government can force a pregnant glue-sniffer into treatment to protect the health of her foetus, a case with implications for abortion rights.

The Manitoba Court of Appeals, citing earlier Supreme Court decisions that a foetus is not a person, had ordered that the woman be allowed to leave an addiction-treatment programme. The Winnipeg Child and Family Services agency appealed.
The Supreme Court gave no reasons for its decision to hear the case. If it had refused to hear the appeal, the previous judgment freeing the woman would have automatically stood.
The court will have to consider, among other issues, the legal status of the unborn child and whether a mother is obligated to care for her foetus.
The Winnipeg agency appealed because two of the woman's three other children were born with a chemical addiction and were developmentally handicapped. The agency had to care for the children.
A lower court had ordered the woman, in her early 20s, into an addiction treatment programme on Aug. 6 but the appeals court reversed this on Sept. 12.

Canada has been without an abortion law since 1988, when the Supreme Court struck down provisions of the criminal code on the grounds that they violated the "liberty and security of the person." The Conservative government at the time pushed a new bill regulating abortion through the elected House of Commons but this was rejected in January 1991 by the unelected Senate and the government then dropped the matter.

The Manitoba appeals court ruled: "The mother's right to sniff solvents may not seem of much importance, but I do not see how a court can select which conduct harmful to an unborn child should be restrained and which not."
With the woman's baby due in December, the Supreme Court will have to act fast if it is to have a practical effect in this case rather than merely establishing legal precedent.
Parties on both sides of the abortion debate were expected to seek to present their arguments to the court, in addition to the Winnipeg agency and the woman's lawyer.
